This paper introduces a novel regression framework for analyzing count time series data: the time-varying Poisson autoregressive (TVAR) model. In this approach, time-varying regression coefficients are estimated using a Gibbs sampler, with coefficient dynamics governed by an additive process. The resulting inference framework allows for the identification of structural shifts and the detection of significant events within the data. The efficacy of the TVAR model is validated through a case study analyzing monthly US airline passenger counts over 47 years, contrasting it with established count time series methodologies. Comparative analyses indicate that the proposed approach outperforms existing methods in both fitting accuracy and one-step-ahead forecasting. Furthermore, the model effectively identifies key historical events, such as the post-World War II economic boom and the oil crises of the 1970s.

Precise measurements of interstellar dust are crucial for comprehending its physical and chemical characteristics, as well as the processes driving its evolution. While techniques like spectroscopy, photometric reddening, and direct imaging are commonly employed for these measurements, they often encounter difficulties in specific scenarios. For instance, low signal-to-noise ratios in faint observations, the difficulty in selecting appropriate comparison spectra for spectroscopy, and the inherent limitations of the "assumed constant variation" method used in photometric reddening can hinder accuracy. Additionally, direct imaging is generally unfeasible for gas-phase observations. To overcome these obstacles, we introduce an innovative technique that derives precise dust opacity measurements using stellar photometry. This method leverages the well-calibrated, linear relationship between stellar photometry and luminosity to function as a stellar spectrophotometer. We have successfully applied this new approach to the Milky Way and Magellanic Clouds, yielding robust dust opacity data with minimal uncertainties.

Comprehensive experiments conducted on systems of varying scales demonstrate that StSEL achieves near-ideal molecular simulation with minimal bias, all while maintaining robust configurational sampling efficiency across diverse materials. These findings indicate that StEL and StSEL serve as superior integrators for simulating systems governed by harmonic forces and offer a powerful, adaptable mechanism for enhancing conformational exploration in molecular dynamics simulations of proteins and other large biomolecules.

Automatic caption generation for images has been the focus of significant research, yet the available evaluation metrics for assessing these captions often fall short. While current metrics like BLEU and CIDER were created to offer a quick and simple way to measure how well an automatic system conveys image content using natural language, they were not specifically designed to incorporate human insights regarding description quality. Consequently, the authors of this study investigate whether integrating subjective quality scores into existing objective metrics can enhance their effectiveness. First, we examine various methods for embedding human quality assessments into current models, ultimately recommending a specific approach that yields superior outcomes compared to alternatives. Subsequently, we explore how different image-caption alignment metrics perform when conditioned on these quality-based scores. Our findings indicate that incorporating human perspective significantly benefits the evaluation of semantic fidelity and content completeness, particularly for metrics like SPICE and ObjectCount. However, for image-region recall measures such as METEOR and ROUGE-L, the advantage is less pronounced. Overall, this research demonstrates that integrating subjective quality scores into current objective evaluations is a viable strategy, especially when assessing descriptions that prioritize semantic accuracy and comprehensive content coverage.

The discovery of a significant positive charge excess in helium-4 (⁴He) produced via photodisintegration of deuterium at low energies has triggered a re-examination of reaction models and nuclear structure theories. This anomaly, which stands at approximately 1.4 times the statistical uncertainty, cannot be reconciled with current reaction frameworks, even when incorporating recent updates to nuclear reaction cross-sections and nucleon and alpha-particle form factors. Consequently, we hypothesize the presence of additional, unaccounted-for particles in reaction channels involving light nuclei. By fitting reaction models to experimental datasets that exclude the anomalous ⁴He result, we derive new predictions for other reactions where such hidden particles could manifest. These predictions indicate the formation of negative-charge analogs of the suspected excess particles in reactions yielding light nuclei with negative parity states, specifically tritium (³H), helium-3 (³He), and lithium-6 (⁶Li). Furthermore, our analysis suggests that reactions producing light nuclei with positive parity states may also generate similar charge anomalies, although these would likely be much smaller and thus harder to detect experimentally.

This study presents the system formulation for Broadband Waveforming Forged Equivalents (BBWF-FE), designed to replicate the capabilities of SISO-OFDM and MISO-OFDM configurations utilizing BBWF-FE. The foundational principles of BBWF-FE, along with the theoretical framework establishing the validity of the BBWF-FG (Broadband WF Forg) for SISO-OFDM and MISO-OFDM scenarios, are comprehensively detailed. To substantiate the theoretical claims, numerical analyses are provided, demonstrating the efficacy of the BBWF-FG (BBWF Forg) in emulating both OFDM architectures while simultaneously illustrating the superior performance of BBWF-FE when compared against traditional single carrier multi-antenna approaches regarding their ability to deliver data and power concurrently.

Precise parton distribution function (parton PDF) inputs are crucial for ensuring the predictive accuracy of the proton PDF model within the framework of Quantum Chromodynamics (QCD). As a statistical Bayesian approach, this model presents a comprehensive solution to the uncertainties inherent in parton PDFs. Bayes' theorem serves as the foundational logic for this framework, formally expressing how prior knowledge, likelihood functions, and prior distributions combine to yield a posterior probability density. This paper offers a detailed exposition of the Bayesian model for parton PDFs, clarifying the specific roles played by each component. We illustrate how the framework systematically integrates various data types, measurement precisions, and theoretical interpretations to refine parton PDF predictions.

This study presents a computational investigation into the reaction of a 20\,cm diameter, 1\,bar, methane air-turbulent jet fire to acoustic excitation generated by an active burner tip. The simulation employs a linearized approach to model an active flame control strategy, which was previously validated against experimental data from the same configuration. The analysis focuses on a single-mode acoustic response to heat flux variations induced by an active tip, operating under a Mach number of 0.1. Results indicate that the linearized model accurately predicts the reaction of the fire to thermal excitation at the burner tip. Specifically, the simulation demonstrates a reduction in the mass flow rate and a corresponding increase in the jet's velocity upon excitation. These findings align closely with experimental observations, confirming the validity of linearized active flame models for predicting the reaction of gas-turbulent fires to acoustic excitation.

Nonlocal gravitation theory represents a covariant, metric-independent formulation of Einstein's nonlinear, self-interacting, and objective gravitational field theory. In this framework, the gravitational field is conceptualized as an objective, symmetric, and nonlocal connection, which is distinct from and not necessarily aligned with the constitutive connection associated with spacetime metric connections. This nonlocal connection is mathematically defined by a constitutive relation that involves the essential tetrads—also referred to as the nonlocal metric itself. These essential tetrads are determined via a nonlocal, objective, and unique constitutive relationship derived from the connection, functioning as the field variables within a first-gradient, covariant, and variational formulation of nonlocal gravitation. This approach parallels how classical general relativity treats linearized, metric-based gravitational theories. The paper provides a detailed exposition of the nonlocal metric, essential tetrads, and the resulting nonlocal geometry, along with their fundamental properties. Additionally, it explores the nonlocal Riemann tensor, defined as the Riemann curvature constructed from the essential tetrads (nonlocal metric), and clarifies the relationship between the Riemann tensor formed by the local metric and that generated by the nonlocal metric.

The LHC experiments are currently analyzing the debris from ultra-relativistic proton collisions to uncover new physics, with a primary focus on the properties of the Standard Model and the discovery of new particles and phenomena. These analyses demand exceptional precision in reconstruction and identification, which are often complicated by the vast quantities of data and the extreme initial conditions created by the tiny system sizes. In this paper, we examine the characteristics of these small systems, exploring how they influence the initial conditions and the subsequent particle production mechanisms.

We examine the intervals between transients in X-ray emitting neutron star (NS) binary systems, analyzing them via the lens of the recurrence times of close stellar encounters near the Galactic plane. These durations are governed by the collective gravitational influence of the Galactic disk and bulge, which periodically lift stars from the plane, causing their associated accretion rates to decline and potentially triggering outbursts in active binaries. We demonstrate that the integral of the luminosity function for neutron star binaries in the vicinity of the Galactic Centre is dominated by low-luminosity systems. This finding indicates that the majority of X-ray binaries hosting neutron stars and located near the Galactic Centre are currently in a quiescent state, a status that may be responsible for the scarcity of identified low-luminulation transients in the inner Galaxy.

Bipartite vertex subdivision involves transforming a bipartite graph $G$ by first performing an arbitrary subdivision on its edges and subsequently redefining the resulting structure as a new bipartite graph. Although the concept is straightforward, providing a formalized definition and establishing the corresponding algorithmic framework demand considerable rigor. This article offers a precise definition of bipartite subdivision along with an efficient algorithm designed to resolve the associated problem of rebalancing partitioning. Specifically, the proposed method functions as a FPT (Fixed-Parameter Tractable) algorithm when parameterized by the imbalance between the newly created bipartite sets. The algorithm executes with a running time of $O(n + m)$, where $n$ represents the count of original vertices in the initial graph and $m$ denotes the total edges processed during subdivision.

In an internal lab setting, we developed HyperDegrade, a remote CPU performance degradation tool designed for an adversary's use. This approach enables an attacker to diminish the computational throughput of a specific target application, causing the victim's measured performance to mirror what would be observed if the program were running at significantly lower CPU clock speeds. The resulting application slowdowns are so pronounced that they facilitate the exposure of top-secret cryptographic keys and other high-entropy secret data. We evaluated HyperDegrade across various workloads, including those with cryptographic keys, machine learning models, and general applications. Our results indicate that the method is effective against AES-256, reducing its key-exposure rate from 2.5 GB/s to 0.0002 GB/s when degrading a 32-core Intel Xeon E5-4620 v4 system from 2.4 GHz to 0.4 GHz. Additionally, we examined HyperDegrade's ability to compromise machine learning models trained to identify faces and detect weapons, as well as its utility in breaching secret application sandboxing mechanisms. We anticipate that this research will inspire further exploration into performance degradation techniques for enhancing cybersecurity and privacy protocols.

Unknotting a closed curve in Euclidean 3-space constitutes a fundamental problem within knot theory, a field with significant applications in chemistry, biology, and materials science. This article offers a fresh perspective on the unknotting process for both traditional and welded unknots. First, the authors introduce a specific class of singularities termed "whisker crossings" and demonstrate how to modify the diagram of a given knot to incorporate these singularities. Subsequently, they establish the main theorem, proving that an increasing sequence of whisker crossings is sufficient to resolve any traditional or welded knot into the unknot. Finally, utilizing this primary result, the paper defines two distinct polynomial invariants applicable to diagrams containing a single whisker crossing.

This study introduces a strategic framework for the coordination of a single high-end agent, or "leader," alongside multiple resource-constrained agents, or "followers," tasked with observing and estimating a target within a stochastic environment. The leader compensates for the followers' limited computational power, memory, and bandwidth by performing complex data fusion and decision-making. We evaluate various agent topologies, analyzing how spatial arrangement and communication protocols influence collective performance. Findings reveal that the team's overall effectiveness hinges on the specific observation strategies employed by the followers and the information fusion techniques utilized by the leader. Notably, the proposed approach delivers substantial gains in estimation accuracy compared to scenarios lacking collaboration, while simultaneously reducing the communication load required by the constrained agents.

We introduce the application of the Cartesian decomposition technique to establish the commutativity of the second fundamental group within the product of garland complexes. This approach relies on decomposing the fundamental group of a lifted garland complex into a sequence of subgroups, each isomorphic to an additive factor inside the fundamental group of a constituent complex. The resulting theorem serves to extend the celebrated theorem by Bridson and Haefliger regarding the commutativity of higher-dimensional higher fundamental subgroups for product spaces of simply connected complexes.

The detection of gravitational wave (GW) signatures demands exceptional sensitivity from sensitive interferometric telescopes, which currently operate near the fundamental thermal noise constraints. Enhancing sensitivity across the high-frequency spectrum is crucial for observing compact binary neutron star (CBNs) mergals prior to a GW detection and for measuring masses of stochastic GW sources. Furthermore, it aids in reducing quantum shot noise that limits sensitivity at frequencies above 500 Hz. While active feedback techniques have already corrected mirror thermal displacements in the Hafele–Weber (HL) configuration down to 200 Hz, further improvements require new designs capable of active correction at higher frequencies. Here, we propose the Sagnach-slosh (SS) telescope, a novel architecture enabling remote, active compensation of thermal noise without modifying the main HL design. Utilizing a Sagnach configuration, the SS telescope creates an on-demand GW signal accessible to standard photodetection methods used in HL. By combining a new "Sagnach-Slosh" signal recycling mirror and feedback control, the SS achieves 10-fold greater sensitivity at 1,000 Hz compared to HL, delivering significant advancements in GW detection capabilities.

Extremely large-scale Multiple-Access (XL-MIMO) systems are poised to be a key enabling technology for sixth-generation (6G) wireless networks. Driven by their vast physical dimensions, these systems face unique challenges regarding user distribution and resource allocation, which are further complicated by the extensive coverage area. Addressing these issues, this paper introduces a novel access protocol designed for XL-MIMO environments that integrates non-intersecting visibility regions with stochastic scheduling. The proposed scheme ensures fair service delivery to all users while maximizing overall system throughput. Specifically, the protocol leverages Non-intersecting Visibility Areas (NIVAs) to eliminate redundant resource allocations caused by overlapping visibility zones. Additionally, a stochastic scheduling component is employed to optimize resource assignment within the NIVAs. To handle the analytical complexities arising from the high-dimensional nature of XL-MIMO, an asymptotic analysis is conducted to derive closed-form approximations for the NIVAs' coverage probability and the system's total throughput. Numerical results demonstrate that the proposed approach significantly enhances system throughput compared to traditional scheduling methods and validates the tightness of the derived asymptotic approximations.

Although neural network language models have largely supplanted traditional approaches, this study finds that the k-gram method remains a viable option for specific applications. We introduce a new framework enabling language neural networks to be trained using k-gram models, which allows the former to capture higher-order patterns while inheriting the efficiency and established corpus availability associated with the latter. Experiments conducted on TIMIT, PTB, and Librispeech demonstrate the effectiveness of this hybrid approach: when a standard top-20, quinquagesimal (5-gram) model is utilized for pre-processing neural data, it boosts TTS performance on TIMIT by 3.1% in WER compared to training purely neural networks without it, and similar gains appear in Librispeech. These outcomes indicate that integrating k-grams into the education of language neural networks can substantially enhance speech recognition outcomes.

This study introduces the iOCR framework, an intelligent image-based ballot counting tool designed to enhance the reliability of optical recognition during election tallies. The method integrates human-in-the-loop corrections to mitigate common errors caused by poor-quality scans or problematic Optical Character Recognition (OCR) interpretations. Specifically, the system employs a multi-stage filtering process: it first utilizes a deep learning classifier to identify suboptimal image-OCR pairings, and subsequently applies a specialized deep neural network trained on corrected datasets to automatically amend the textual extraction from problematic ballots. Evaluations conducted on simulated 2020 US election counts, which incorporated various image degradation techniques, demonstrated that this informed approach significantly outperformed standard OCR methods. When compared against baseline systems using the 2020 New York primary election dataset, iOCR achieved a 99.99% match rate with the official certified results. These findings indicate that the framework offers a robust, dependable solution for ensuring accuracy in automated vote tabulation.

Hydrodynamic theories provide a low-energy effective description of many-body systems, yet standard approaches often fall short for quantum fluids, particularly when addressing non-equilibrium dynamics or high-energy regimes. To overcome these constraints, we introduce a novel hydrodynamic framework for a quantum fluid in the presence of interactions, built upon the Phase-Space Random Quantum Hydrodynamics (PSRQHD) formalism. This approach models the non-local constitutive relations of the constitutive model as a function of a non-Markovian memory kernel, which encapsulates the influence of higher-order moments. By formulating a closed set of equations through an approximation of this kernel, our framework achieves a closed description involving only density and velocity fields. We demonstrate that this closed system aligns with the Gross-Pitaevskii (GP) equations under specific conditions, allowing for the study of non-equilibrium dynamics via the derivation of an equivalent closed real-space equation for the wavefunction. This resulting real-space equation mirrors the structure of the Nakajima-Suzuki master equation, featuring a dissipative term and an additional non-linear contribution. We further demonstrate that our closed hydrodynamic equations are mathemematically equivalent to those derived by Baym and Kadanoff, confirming the consistency of our approach with established formulations.

Evaluation of automated assessment systems for subjective tests like those used in school or university exams relies heavily on objective criteria. Specifically, schools and universities typically employ either structured item types, such as multiple-choice or fill-in-the-blouse questions, or paired-permutation items, where two students' responses are compared by an expert to determine equivalence, with final scores calculated based on these decisions. To enhance the reliability of these item-based evaluations, various methods have been proposed, yet current automated items often fail to capture nuanced grading variations. Consequently, there is a pressing requirement for robust evaluation techniques suitable for school and university item tests. This study introduces a new method designed for precise scoring of paired-permutation item assessments, formally termed the Precise Paired-Permutation Examination (PPRE). The ppre algorithm functions as an adaptive search strategy that reconstructs the original ranking of answers within the paired-permutation format. The proposed approach guarantees an exact reconstruction of the hidden answer order with a time complexity of $O(n \log n)$ for tests containing $n$ distinct responses. Validation through both simulated data and real-world datasets demonstrates that the ppre algorithm significantly outperforms standard item tests, thereby offering a superior tool for evaluating automated assessment models in K-12 and higher education contexts.

Specifically, detection occurs at grid points via deterministic or stochastic binary decisions regarding presence, with lattice targets generating positive detections while non-lattice ones result in negative detections. Although the resulting filter involves infinite sums, approximations transform it into a computationally practical form. The algorithm's application in optimizing sensor allocation strategies for detection tasks is also investigated.

Soccer stands out among team sports for the extensive statistical analysis performed on matches and games, a practice known as match statistics. The primary objective of these statistics is to extract insights that can be utilized to enhance the performance of the analyzed team. Consequently, the vast majority of statistical studies concentrate on the retrospective examination of matches to identify correlations between specific game events and their outcomes. Conversely, the prediction of match results based on statistical data typically employs probabilistic models or machine learning algorithms. In this research, the objective of integrating statistics is explored through a novel statistical framework designed for a strategic approach within soccer, which is enhanced and subsequently utilized to train a reinforcement learning model. This learning system is applied to the top-tier Italian professional soccer league, Serie A, to investigate the decision-making processes of managers during the most critical moments of a game. The findings indicate that the strategic decisions derived from this learning system align closely with the actual choices made by real-life managers. Furthermore, the simulation results demonstrate that the decisions generated by this learning model are superior to those resulting from traditional statistical methods.

Driven by the rapid evolution of technology, Laser Doppler Vibrometry (LDV) has emerged as a premier technique for non-contact, full-field vibration analysis. While scanning LDVs mitigate the need for extensive manual movement, they often incur prohibitive costs and complex configurations. To resolve these challenges, this study introduces an affordable solution utilizing a single, standard LDV unit configured for two-dimensional mapping via a remote-controlled single-point system. The approach involves a compact, user-friendly assembly that integrates a simple optical arrangement with a motorized stage, enabling the acquisition of 2D vibration data from a wide field of view. Validation of this method was conducted on an aluminum cantilever beam under various boundary conditions and excitation frequencies. Results demonstrated that the distant, single-point setup delivers 2D results comparable in quality to those obtained with a direct-view scanning LDV.

These biases stem from the inversion algorithms themselves, as well as from the physical characteristics of the observed spectral lines and the instrumental setup. In this paper, we introduce a comprehensive model that incorporates the differential measurement principle, the specific characteristics of the inversion algorithm, and the known biases associated with solar spectral lines and instrumentation. Utilizing this model, we conduct a detailed investigation into the origins of these biases and their collective impact on the resulting magnetic field measurements. Our analysis reveals that the most significant contributor to the measured component is the "concentration bias," arising from the fact that polarized signal inversion techniques rely on the assumption that the measured spectral line intensity accurately reflects the total magnetic flux. We further demonstrate that this concentration bias is not merely a theoretical artifact but manifests as a genuine physical effect in the data. Finally, we explore the current strategies available to mitigate these biases and project future advancements in both observational capabilities and inversion methodologies.

This paper offers a comprehensive exploration of the concept of Bertrand curves within the context of timelike curves in semi-Riemannian spaces. We establish a characterization theorem for these specific timelike Bertrand curves, referred to as "Timelike Bertrand Curves" (TBCs), and provide a detailed analysis of their associated Frenet frames. Furthermore, we examine the relationship between TBCs and other curve types, including those with pseudo-orthogonal Frenet frames, as well as helices and general space curves. Finally, the study includes the construction of various examples illustrating these curves.

This study investigates whether modifying the loss function from categorical cross-entropy to a weighted variant offers advantages for deep neural networks used in multi-class classification. Specifically, the authors explore if such a change mitigates biases toward majority classes, a common challenge when dealing with imbalanced datasets. The research employs a series of deep learning models trained on both natural image datasets and a medical imaging dataset of retinal fundus images to test this hypothesis. Results indicate that while weighted losses are theoretically designed to address class imbalance, they do not inherently provide a benefit in these contexts. Instead, the findings reveal that simply adjusting the weighting scheme can sometimes increase bias against minority classes. Ultimately, the paper concludes that for deep learning classifiers, the specific weight assignment is more influential than the mere act of moving from an unweighted to a weighted loss function.

We introduce ATOMIC, a new knowledge representation framework designed to encode conditional reasoning in artificial intelligence systems. This approach enables machines to replicate the kind of analogical and other forms of inference that humans perform effortlessly when making decisions based on "if-then" logic. ATOMIC builds an explicit library of shared reasoning patterns across AI models, allowing for the extraction of these commonalities to foster a form of collective machine knowledge. The system ingests conditional information from diverse datasets, constructs a structured atlas of these inferences, and utilizes it to introduce new conditional facts or correct existing ones. Evaluations demonstrate that ATOMIC significantly boosts the inclusion of new knowledge in target datasets, as well as the correction of erroneous inferences already present.

Video prediction represents a cutting-edge technology with wide-ranging applications, yet it remains notoriously difficult to master. This study introduces a novel framework called Dual-Rep, designed to enhance video prediction by addressing the inherent complexity of modeling diverse object interactions and unpredictable environmental changes. At the heart of Dual-Rep is a distinctive dual-representation strategy that decouples foreground dynamics from static backgrounds. By employing a simple yet effective generative model to reconstruct the background, the framework concentrates its predictive capabilities solely on foreground elements. Furthermore, to manage the vast variety of potential future configurations, the model utilizes an ensemble of predictors operating within a latent space. Comprehensive evaluations conducted on three standard benchmarks—MPO, FiD, and FiG—demonstrate that Dual-Rep consistently outperforms current state-of-the-art methods. Specifically, on the MPO dataset, the proposed approach surpassed previous records by a significant 14%, while also delivering measurable improvements on Fisher Discrimination tasks involving figure ground detection.

The metric dimension of a graph represents the smallest possible size for a resolving set for the entire graph. This study focuses on the so-called weak metric dimension, or shortened metric dimension, which is defined as the minimum number of vertices required to resolve all shortest path lengths within a specific subgraph. Formally, a subset $U$ serves as a weak resolution for a subgraph $H$ if there exists a unique mapping from the vertex set to the Cartesian power of $U$ such that the distance between any two vertices in $H$ can be determined by comparing their respective shortest path lengths to the elements of $U$; the union of all such subsets $U$ constitutes the weak resolution for $H$. This concept extends naturally to weighted graphs as well. In this paper, we establish the relationship between the standard metric dimension and the weak (or shortened) metric dimension for a general subgraph $H$ of a finite graph. Additionally, we derive the precise formula for the shortened metric dimension applicable to cycles, unions of cycles, and subdivided cycles. Finally, the article provides a characterization for the shortened metric dimension of finite trees and explores its application in determining the metric dimension of a finite graph based on its cycle cover.

The primary objective of this study is to develop a novel deep learning architecture designed for heart sound (HS) analysis, specifically targeting the binary classification of normal heart sounds (N) and pathological heart sounds (P). This class-based categorization is crucial for early disease detection, thereby facilitating effective treatment strategies. To address the scarcity of labeled datasets, the proposed architecture integrates self-supervised learning techniques. The method employs a hierarchical framework consisting of two primary stages: first, a base unsupervised model extracts latent representations from raw heart sounds, and second, a supervised classifier utilizes these features for categorization. Furthermore, the architecture incorporates a specialized module capable of mitigating additive noise and another dedicated to managing geometric distortions arising from image deformation. Validated against two distinct heart sound datasets, the results demonstrate that the suggested method significantly outperforms existing state-of-the-art approaches, achieving 98.4% accuracy on Dataset 1 and 89.1% on Dataset 2.

We present a new Monte Carlo algorithm designed to simulate the asymmetric simple exclusion process (ASEP) by treating it as a discrete-time, discrete-space driven lattice gas. In this framework, the system evolves under a stochastic local update rule where particles attempt to move forward with position-dependent rates, subject to the constraint that they cannot occupy the same site. These attempted moves are accepted only if the resulting configuration lowers the system's energy, defined by an external, site-specific field. By carefully selecting these fields, one can precisely reproduce the original continuous-time, continuous-space dynamics of ASEP. Although the proposed procedure is not time-reversible, we demonstrate that it remains ergodic and converges to the unique stationary state characteristic of the process.

These mathematical representations rely on specific assumptions regarding the biological characteristics of the pathogen and the available data, which must be explicitly stated to ensure clarity and reproducibility. Furthermore, because numerous distinct approaches exist for simulating outbreaks, selecting the most suitable framework for a given scenario is crucial. This selection process should be guided by the unique attributes of the disease under investigation and the objectives of the specific analysis. Although the choice of an appropriate model for the ongoing SARS-CoV-2 epidemic remains a subject of debate, it is imperative that the chosen framework aligns with the available evidence and the intended purpose of the study.

This research investigates cross-language sentiment analysis for the domain of Chinese restaurant reviews, aiming to generate a dataset that fills existing gaps. The study introduces a proposed model designed to facilitate multi-task learning for sentiment classification across languages. The proposed approach incorporates an additional task specifically aimed at mitigating sentiment label noise, which is prevalent in unsupervised cross-language sentiment analysis. Furthermore, the method employs a distributional sentiment representation to effectively integrate unsupervised target language data within a deep neural network architecture. Evaluated using an newly developed dataset, the results indicate that the proposed approach significantly outperforms current state-of-the-art methods in both supervised and unsupervised settings.

The rapid proliferation of social media has significantly amplified the reach of news, yet it has simultaneously facilitated the distribution of deceptive content, including fake news. While often associated with misinformation, deception on these platforms can also be intentional, serving purposes such as advertising, political campaigning, or mere entertainment. Furthermore, the user base frequently encounters not only deliberate lies but also unintentional inaccuracies, collectively termed "deception." To address these challenges, research has concentrated on developing detection systems. However, existing approaches face limitations regarding data scarcity and the difficulty of collecting labeled examples for various forms of deceptive content. Additionally, current models struggle to adapt to emerging types of news deception, as they lack the ability to generalize detection capabilities for newly introduced deception strategies. To resolve these issues, we propose a framework for detecting news deception that is label-free, data-efficient, and capable of generalizing across new deceptive strategies. Our approach integrates multimodal analysis with an emergent counter detection mechanism through a process learning framework. Empirical results demonstrate that our method effectively identifies news deception, surpassing current state-of-the-art performance by 11\% when tested on real-world datasets.

The concept of Golay complementary structures (GCs) has attracted significant interest due to their exceptional spectral characteristics, which facilitate the creation of filters with nearly ideal passband and stopband responses. Building upon GCs, polyphase Golay complementary structures (PGCSs) were introduced to enhance spectral properties, yet existing PGCSs face constraints regarding design flexibility and applicability. This paper presents two novel configurations designed to overcome these limitations: a general framework for PGCSs is established, and within it, two distinct designs are formulated. The first configuration enables the construction of PGCSs involving arbitrary-order low-pass GC pairs, while the second facilitates combinations of GCs with disparate lengths. Simulation results demonstrate that both proposed structures effectively achieve target responses for various communication applications, including orthogonal frequency-division multiplexing (OFDM) peak-to-average ratio reduction and multi-carrier code-division multiple-access (MC-CDMA) gain.

Detecting these lesions is vital for clinical decision-making, yet existing deep learning architectures often falter because they are trained on datasets where healthy brains and those with lesions are combined into a single input stream. Standard convolutional neural networks (CNNs) typically process such data as a monolithic entity, which hinders their ability to distinguish between normal anatomy and pathological features. This generator produces a binary mask indicating the presence of abnormalities, which is then evaluated by an adversarial classifier to drive iterative improvements. Attribute extraction serves as a crucial preprocessing technique for attribute recognition, yet existing specialized models for attribute extraction often fail to adapt effectively to new attributes due to their rigid architectures. Conversely, general-purpose models designed for other tasks possess flexible frameworks capable of accommodating new attributes but lack the precision required for attribute extraction. To bridge this divide, we introduce a unified architecture that integrates both recognition and adaptable attributes into a single, cohesive model. This approach employs a contrastive learning paradigm to simultaneously optimize attribute recognition and the adaptability of attribute selection. Within this framework, the contrastive objective functions are reconfigured to incorporate an attribute selection module, which is trained specifically to enhance the model's adaptability. Extensive experiments conducted on four distinct datasets demonstrate that this proposed architecture not only achieves superior performance in attribute extraction and recognition compared to current state-of-the-art methods but also exhibits remarkable adaptability when handling new attributes.

Large language models (LLMs) have garnered significant attention due to their exceptional capabilities across a wide range of tasks. Although fine-tuning is a common approach to enhance these abilities, it is often resource-intensive and computationally expensive. As an alternative, post-hoc methods like prompt engineering and in-context learning (ICL) allow users to leverage an existing model's potential without retraining. However, for very large models where ICL offers diminishing returns, fine-tuning remains the preferred option. This study introduces SKILL—a novel, efficient framework designed to upgrade an llm by integrating a larger target model. The process involves first distilling knowledge from the target into the base llm to create an intermediate representation, which is subsequently refined using direct interaction with the target model. Remarkably, this two-step procedure eliminates the need for additional data or further adjustments. Evaluations demonstrate that a 7B parameter model enhanced via SKILL using an LLaMA-30B target achieves performance comparable to models that have been extensively fine-tuned, surpassing both standard ICL approaches and single-step distillation methods.

Quantum entanglement and quantum synchronization are two non-classical phenomena that are crucial for the development of quantum technologies. This paper investigates how the transformation of entanglement can precipitate the emergence of synchronization. Specifically, we analyze the entanglement-assisted synchronization of classical continuous variables within the W, thermal, and coherent states of light. Our findings reveal that the entanglement between the x and p quadratures of two coherent states, when these states serve as inputs for a phase-insensitive amplifier involving W, thermal, or coherent light, is converted into synchronization between the x and p variables of the resulting tomographic outputs. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the synchronization of x and p variables in the reconstructed image can be achieved even when entanglement is absent in the original input states.

This article addresses the challenge of constructing the submodule lattice for a specific class of modules over a Lie algebra, which possess a finite, well-known basis and are defined by a multiplicity-free property. The approach relies exclusively on combinatorial data derived from the target modules themselves, as mandated by Birkhoff's theorem. Ultimately, the resulting construction is expressed as a poset structure built upon the original module's basis, with an order relation determined by the Poincaré polynomial and a newly introduced, combinatorially defined function.

Neural networks trained to classify LiDAR point clouds frequently encounter difficulties with overfitting, a problem that can be alleviated by smoothing techniques adapted from natural language processing. These methods average embedding representations within a k-nearest neighbors framework before feeding them into a neural classifier. However, existing smoothing approaches face two primary constraints: they rely on the assumption that the embedding space is Euclidean, and they operate under the premise that the embedding of a transformed point cloud remains invariant to that specific transformation. The first constraint limits their applicability to models with Euclidean-compatible layers, such as PointNet, whereas the second restricts their utility to specific geometric changes like rotation and scaling. To overcome these barriers, we introduce Transformation-Point Cloud (TPC), a novel smoothing method applicable to any neural network architecture without requiring Euclidean assumptions or invariance to transformations. Our approach first trains a model to predict specific transformation types and their associated parameters using points that have been altered. Subsequently, the smoothing process involves averaging the embeddings of the original points plus those of their transformed counterparts. We validate the effectiveness of TPC across various architectures and under diverse transformations through both synthetic experiments and real-world applications, demonstrating superior performance compared to current methods.

This study introduces a novel approach to programming contests, designed to evaluate the problem-solving capabilities of participants. The proposed method is entirely automated, requiring no human intervention during the assessment process. The core of the system is an algorithm that constructs a comprehensive graph representing all submitted solutions for a specific problem. This graph-based model enables the automatic identification of the most effective solution for each task. The validity and practicality of the proposed method were demonstrated through the analysis of problems from the 2014 Chinese Collegiate Programming Contest.

This result is applied to establish the "clear" form of the Serre weights for the crystalline representations with Hodge--Tate weights $\{0,1\}$ and a specific regularity condition on the associated filtration, requiring only a finite verification. Additionally, we provide an explicit description of the "clear" forms for the $\ell$-adic ordinary representations for primes $\ell \neq p$ under analogous conditions.

Active Shape Control (ASC) represents a cutting-edge active technique designed to mitigate unwanted vibrations in structures equipped with self-sensing composite materials. This study introduces an innovative strategy to reconstruct the spatially varying, anisotropic conductivity tensor within fiber-reinforced composites. The methodology integrates physical constraints derived from the governing differential equations and their associated boundary conditions into a purely surface-based inversion algorithm. Complementing this, an experimental framework combining electrical impedance tomography and ASC is utilized to demonstrate the efficacy of the tensor reconstruction method specifically tailored for GFRP (glass fiber-reinforced polymer) materials. Subsequently, the precise conductivity anisotropy is derived from the established exact solution of the three-dimensional, frequency-dependent conductivity tensor. The resulting model enables the simultaneous determination of principal conductivity orientations and magnitudes for both isotropic and anisotropic fiber composites. Notably, the proposed approach requires no prior knowledge of the material's constitutive properties, rendering it fully non-parametric.

Distributed decision-making in dynamic environments is crucial for high-stakes applications like autonomous driving and robotic exploration. This paper addresses the distributional linear bandit problem, where an agent must select actions to optimize an unknown linear reward function. In a strict decision-theoretic framework, a single learner (the agent) interacts with an environment, contrasting with a practical scenario for intelligent systems where an algorithm operates within a team of collaborating agents. Here, a reward function is collectively learned through a network of agents, each possessing unique characteristics and facing distinct reward structures. The communication protocol involves agents transmitting only their selected actions and observed rewards to a central learner, who computes the optimal strategy and conveys it back to the agents for execution. We introduce a novel distributed algorithm designed for this framework, which combines existing techniques with new innovations to ensure non-asymptotic regret bounds that are near-optimal relative to a fully informed baseline. These limits are shown to be sub-optimal by a logarithmic factor when compared to optimal bounds achievable under standard assumptions. Furthermore, a tight regret bound is established specifically for the cumulative regret incurred by the environment. Empirical results indicate that the proposed algorithm performs effectively in real-world applications, closely approaching the performance of methods with full information.

The outer regions of protoplanetary disks are characterized by low midplane temperatures, enabling the rapid onset of dust growth and the subsequent development of a dust-driven viscosity that enhances angular momentum transport. This process may facilitate the clearing of material in the disk's exterior. The rapid advancement of artificial intelligence and Internet technologies has spurred widespread adoption of machine learning across numerous domains. However, privacy concerns regarding sensitive data, coupled with high costs associated with model retraining, have created significant hurdles in centralized training. To address these issues, Federated Learning (FL) was introduced, enabling distributed training while keeping data local to its source. Despite these benefits, FL still encounters challenges when dealing datasets with non-independent and non-identical (non-IID) distributions. To mitigate the impact of such data heterogeneity, various strategies have been proposed, including k-means clustering, knowledge distillation, and Meta-learning. This paper introduces a novel approach called Stroll for Education (StrollEd), designed to enhance the training of global models when faced with highly diverse data. The StrollEd framework combines the global Meta-learning model with local k-means clustering and distillation techniques. Our experiments demonstrate that StrollEd significantly outperforms existing methods in classification tasks involving image data.

The rapid expansion of medical imaging technology, driven by increasing clinical demand, has created a significant gap between available data and the capacity for manual annotation. Our approach combines a pre-trained convolutional neural network (CNN) with a segmentation module trained exclusively on labeled data. Single-particle quantum mechanics exhibits a form of nonlocality that has been described as "spooky action at a distance," miring the nonlocality found in entangled systems. This paper argues that single-particle nonlocality is actually a manifestation of guidance nonlocality, which arises because the wave function is a physical, nonlocal entity. Drawing an analogy with entangled systems, the authors define single-particle guidance nonlocality as a "signal-nonlocality effect," where the wave function of a probe entangled with a remote system is altered nonlocally via a measurement performed locally at the signal source. To demonstrate guidance nonlocality in single-particle scenarios, the study presents a single-particle version of the Bell-CHSH inequality, showing that guidance nonlocal entanglement can be verified through a Bell test involving two distant detectors and one local preparation unit. Furthermore, the paper establishes a single-particle counterpart to the Yu-Oh inequality, which offers a simpler demonstration of guidance nonlocality than a standard Bell test. Finally, the study suggests guidance nonlocality may help clarify the nonlocal character of the Aharonov-Bohm effect.
